newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan top envoy in mysterious foreign visit.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan top envoy in mysterious foreign visit.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister dropped from sight on Tuesday to embark on what one local newspaper said was yet another overseas mission cloaked in secrecy to evade rival China's tightening diplomatic embargo.

The foreign ministry, adopting the tight-lipped policy seen during previous secret sojourns by Taiwan leaders, said minister John Chang was "out of town for official business" but would not comment on a report he may have gone to west Asia.

The Liberty Times, quoting unidentified sources, said Chang left Taiwan late on Monday for a three-to-four-day visit to some foreign nations that have no diplomatic ties with the island but which nonetheless maintain "secret and close" links.
Chang was likely to head for west Asia and may visit Europe later, the newspaper said.

Chang and Vice President Lien Chan have followed a similar pattern for numerous overseas trips in the past year, simply dropping from sight for days at a time as international and Taiwan media scurried to track them down.
Lien, who doubles as premier, managed such a secret visit to Ukraine in August, triggering a minor diplomatic row between the former Soviet republic and a furious Beijing.

Similarly, Chang dropped from sight after his December visit to South Africa, where he had sought in vain to reverse Pretoria's November 27 decision to switch diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1997.

Chang surfaced in Belgium on December 7 but failed to win access to Belgian leaders or other European or African officials there as Beijing diplomats mounted what Taiwan officials and media said was a concerted drive to prevent such encounters.

Communist China, Taiwan's arch rival since a civil war split them in 1949, regards the island as a rebel province ineligible for sovereign ties and has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in its quest to bring Taiwan under Beijing's rule.
Chang nonetheless said on Monday he would visit diplomatic ally Guatemala for the December 29 signing of a peace pact between the government and leftist rebels.

The trip is one of four damage-control missions planned by top Taiwan officials since Taipei's largest ally, South Africa, reversed its longstanding loyalty and said it would switch ties to Beijing by the end of 1997.
Beijing refuses to recognise any country that recognises Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government but has stepped up efforts to win over the few countries that still do.
